newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Everbright says Beijing must agree asset sale.
newsitem.headline: Everbright says Beijing must agree asset sale.

text.p: The acquisition of mainland China-based assets by a Hong Kong company from its mainland parent required the approval of the ultimate owner, the chairman of the China Everbright Group Ltd said on Thursday.
For many Hong Kong-listed companies with mainland Chinese parents, ownership and control ultimately lie with a state-run agency or the government of a city or province.
"For listed companies in Hong Kong, if they want to acquire assets outside of Hong Kong, I believe that the original owner should approve these acquisitions," said group chairman Zhu Xiaohua.

"Because of the linkage of the parent company in the mainland and the listed company in Hong Kong, (there is) some close relationship, a special shareholder-ownership relationship, (then) we should consider (them) as state assets," said Zhu.
Zhu was speaking at an investment seminar held by Indosuez W.I. Carr Securities in Hong Kong.
Zhu is also chairman of Hong Kong-based China Everbright Holdings Co. Ltd and China Everbright-IHD Pacific Ltd
He also stressed the need for better supervision of asset injections by mainland companies into their listed Hong Kong vehicles.
"I think (in) the disputes between the two sides at the core is improvement of supervision by the mainland authorities," said Zhu. "It is the core issue."
The Hong Kong-listed companies controlled by mainland entities, called red chips by investors in Hong Kong, often have substantial assets that are based in China.

China's securities regulators have been concerned some mainland parent companies may be using Hong Kong corporate vehicles to offer stock and sidestep supervision by Beijing. They are also concerned that state assets may be sold at less than fair prices, yielding a loss of state wealth.
Zhu gave Everbright-IHD's intention to acquire a stake in Everbright Bank of China Ltd as an example of the need for approval by the ultimate owner.

"Even if we acquire the assets from an associate company of Everbright Group Beijing, we should get approval of our share(holding) from the monetary authority, said Zhu. "And another thing, we should report to the state asset administration bureau."
The state asset administration bureau or National Administration of State Property must also approve the sale or transfer of state property in China.

Zhu said Everbright Bank was 51 percent owned by the China Everbright Group Ltd, but the Everbright group was 100 percent owned by the State Council, or cabinet, and any sale of the bank's shares would require approval from the State Council.
The acquisition of a stake in Everbright Bank by the Hong Kong company would also need the approval of the People's Bank of China, the central bank, he said.

Everbright-IHD announced on Thursday it had raised HK$1.88 billion in a placement of new and old shares and that one of the ultimate uses of those funds would be the acquisition of a 20 percent stake in Beijing-based Everbright Bank.
The company had expressed an interest in acquiring a stake in the Beijing-based bank in early 1997, the announcement said.

Relevant government approvals had been requested but not yet received. No negotiations had yet been conducted on price or any other factors of any potential acquisition of the bank by the company and no agreements reached, it said.
Shares of Everbright-IHD soared to an all-time high of HK$18.60 after the issue of the announcement, then eased to close HK$5.70 higher at HK$17.60 on Thursday.
